02

Genre & Conventions

Genre = a category a media product belongs to. A genre is recognisable to audiences through its shared conventions. We identify genre using N.I.C.S.

N.I.C.S — the genre detector

  • Narrative — predictable/formulaic story arcs. Crime drama often uses a flexi-narrative: 2–3 cases or storylines at once.
  • Iconography — objects associated with a genre (police tape, bomb suits, sirens — or cowboy hats in westerns).
  • Characters — stock characters, e.g. the tough rule-breaker cop, the nervous rookie, the crime boss.
  • Setting — where the text is located, e.g. urban streets, police HQ, crime scenes.
The typical crime drama narrative arc: equilibrium → disruption → investigation → complications → climax → resolution

Warming up the words

  • GENRE — the type of media text, e.g. television crime drama.
  • CONVENTIONS — the set of shared characteristics that make a genre recognisable.
  • SUB-GENRE — categories within a genre, e.g. crime drama, family drama.
  • HYBRID GENRE — a mix of 2+ main genres, e.g. horror-comedy. Producers hybridise to appeal to wider audiences.
  • DIEGESIS — "the world in which the story takes place."
  • VERISIMILITUDE — the believability of that world.
Iconography: a high-tech lab instantly signals "USA forensic drama"

Trigger Point's genre: Crime Thriller / Police Procedural (+ bomb disposal drama)

  • A professional specialist protagonist with personal and emotional stakes
  • High-stress, high-risk situations — terrorism, explosives, threats of violence
  • Team dynamics: loyalty, conflict and hierarchy in the police/counter-terror unit
  • Realistic settings — urban streets, police HQ, crime scenes
  • Technical language, procedures and realistic equipment
  • Suspense built through pacing, silence, ticking timers and close calls
  • Moral ambiguity — ethical dilemmas and tough choices
  • Emotional backstories that drive characters' decisions
  • Twists and ongoing investigations to keep the audience hooked
  • Fast-paced editing and dramatic camerawork to heighten urgency

Restricted vs Inverted narrative

Restricted narrative — the audience is given limited information about the crime or characters. We solve it alongside the detective.

Inverted narrative — the criminal is identified early; the pleasure is watching how they'll be caught.

Knives Out shows us early on how Harlan died and who was involved — which narrative type is that closest to?

Steve Neale — Repetition & Difference

Texts need recognisable features to be identified as a genre (repetition) but must also be different so audiences don't get bored. Sort each Trigger Point feature: is it Repetition of crime drama conventions, or a Difference?

A central mystery — who is behind the bombing? — with a clear investigation underway
Less traditional detective work — action-based bomb disposal rather than interviews and forensics
A troubled, brave lead character under constant pressure
The protagonist is an Expo (bomb disposal expert), not a detective
Gritty, realistic urban London setting with institutional locations like police HQ
Some scenes feel more like military-style operations than urban policing
Themes of terrorism, justice, risk and fear; fast editing, handheld camera, tense soundtrack
Greater emphasis on national security and public infrastructure than domestic crime

Characters & Their Situations

Click any card to reveal genre role, costume and representation notes — the three angles the exam loves. Ask yourself: how typical is each character of the crime/thriller genre?

Lana Washington

Vicky McClure
Hero / Protagonist

Bomb disposal expert ("Expo") with the Met. Returns from six months in Estonia training Ukrainian bomb disposal teams — thrust straight back into duty when an explosion rocks central London. Carries psychological scars: the loss of her colleague and her brother.

Genre role: the seasoned professional of high-stakes thrillers — and the "lone wolf" maverick, haunted by trauma and willing to break rules to get results.

Costume: practical bomb-disposal gear — signifies authority, danger and professionalism; eliminates any sense of gendered presentation.

Representation: challenges gender stereotypes — calm under pressure, authoritative, leading in a field traditionally dominated by men.

▼ click for exam detail

DCI Thom Youngblood

Mark Stanley
Authority / Sidekick?

Lana's former romantic partner, now in a relationship with DS Helen Morgan. Unresolved feelings between him and Lana resurface during the crisis.

Genre role: the authoritative figure of crime dramas — overseeing operations, making critical decisions under pressure.

Costume: typically formal, reflecting his high-ranking position in the police force.

Representation: aligns with conventional male leadership roles — a familiar dynamic within the genre.

▼ click for exam detail

Hass Rahim

Nabil Elouahabi
Team / Interim Leader

Previously part of Lana's team; temporarily led the unit during her absence. Works alongside Lana and Danny responding to the bombing in Episode 1.

Genre role: interim lead of the explosives team — the challenges of leadership in crisis, a common thriller theme.

Costume: functional, mirroring his team — emphasising unity and shared danger.

Representation: diversifies leadership roles in the genre — a competent, composed figure in command.

▼ click for exam detail

Danny

Eric Shango
Steadfast Partner

A member of Lana's team, now engaged and more secure in his role since series 1. Works closely with Lana during the Episode 1 crisis.

Genre role: the reliable support — police driver and assistant to the explosives team, providing logistics and mobility.

Costume: standard police attire, high-visibility vest and utility belt — readiness and commitment to duty.

Representation: reinforces traditional male traits of strength, reliability and loyalty; his supportive dynamic with Lana balances gender roles.

▼ click for exam detail

DS Helen Morgan

Natalie Simpson
Investigator

A new addition to the team and Thom's current partner. Plays a significant role in the investigation after the bombing — her relationship with Thom creates personal tension in the team.

Genre role: fresh perspective on the investigative team — analytical skills and dedication, a classic supporting-character trait.

Costume: professional yet understated — blends into the investigative environment.

Representation: part of the growing representation of women in law enforcement — competence and resilience.

▼ click for exam detail

Commander John Francis

Julian Ovenden
Figurehead / Command

Introduced in series 2 to oversee the response to the bombing — his arrival adds authority and scrutiny to the team's operations.

Genre role: the bureaucratic figurehead — highlights tension between field operatives and administrative command.

Costume: suit, tie, badge/lanyard — seniority, authority and distance from the front line: in charge, but not in the action.

Representation: conventional male leadership — control, decisiveness, strategic oversight. His clipped, received-pronunciation delivery contrasts with Lana's London accent, signalling rank and class.

Kris Hitchen
Morally Ambiguous

A key member of the bomb disposal unit with a complicated history — experienced, but often clashes with Lana. His past actions created trust issues within the team.

Genre role: the seasoned officer with a contentious past — unpredictability and conflict that challenge Lana professionally and personally.

Costume: mirrors the other Expos — protective gear and standard-issue uniform, emphasising collective responsibility and risk.

Representation: traditional masculine assertiveness and stoicism — but his misjudgements challenge the infallibility of male authority figures.

04

Representation

Representation = the ways in which the media re-presents the world and aspects of it — social groups, issues and events. Crime dramas are fictional, but they construct a world the audience is asked to believe in. You study representations of gender, ethnicity, age, issues and events.

STEREOTYPES MALE / FEMALE GAZE CHALLENGE CONFORM MEDIATION

How are representations constructed? Through VATLs

  • Technical codes — camera shots, angles and editing all contribute. A low-angle shot can make a character appear intimidating; the camera can position us to feel empathy.
  • Editing — the final edit mediates the representation: what we see is not real life but a constructed version of reality.
  • Audio codes — tense non-diegetic sound can represent a sinister motive.
  • Iconography — a location's backdrop can represent anything from danger to romance.

Warm-up: how are these people represented?

One sentence each — try to use STEREOTYPES, MALE/FEMALE GAZE, CHALLENGE or CONFORM.

Todorov's Narrative Theory — applied to Trigger Point

StageWhat happensTrigger Point S2 E1
1. EquilibriumEverything is fine & peacefulLana is back from Estonia
2. DisruptionThe antagonist upsets the peaceAn explosion in the heart of London
3. RecognitionThe protagonist realises something is wrongThe investigation reveals there are more bombs
4. RepairThe protagonist tries to make things betterThe car park operation to locate the drone operator
5. New equilibriumPeace returns — but with some changeThe immediate threat is sorted… but the bomber is still at large

Character representation profiles — conform or challenge?

Each profile follows the four exam headings: Appearance · Personality · Job/role · Verdict on stereotypes of gender, race and job role.

Lana Washington

Challenges
  • Appearance — practical bomb-disposal gear and protective equipment; her costume eliminates any sense of gendered presentation and signals danger, authority and professionalism.
  • Personality — calm under pressure, determined, willing to break rules; haunted by past trauma (her brother, her colleague).
  • Job/role — Expo and team leader: the hero/protagonist role of the drama.
  • Verdict — strongly challenges gender stereotypes: a woman leading in a high-risk field traditionally given to male characters. She does, however, conform to the job-role trope of the maverick "lone wolf" hero.

John Hudson

Both
  • Appearance — a serious-looking white male in tactical uniform, reflecting his operational role on the ground.
  • Personality — cold, blunt and dismissive, especially toward Lana — a lack of trust or respect for her judgement.
  • Job/role — experienced EOD operative but not in leadership; his attitude creates tension and rivalry in the team.
  • Verdict — conforms to the tough, emotionally distant male and stereotypical resistance to female authority — but challenges job-role stereotypes by being flawed and unlikable rather than heroic; his death in the explosion subverts the idea that toughness guarantees survival.

DCI Thom Youngblood

Conforms
  • Appearance — typically formal attire, reflecting his high-ranking position in the police force.
  • Personality — authoritative decision-maker under pressure, but emotionally compromised by unresolved feelings for Lana.
  • Job/role — senior detective overseeing operations — the familiar authority figure of crime drama.
  • Verdict — largely conforms to conventional male leadership roles, providing a familiar genre dynamic; the emotional entanglement adds a small crack in the stoic-male stereotype.

Hass Rahim

Challenges
  • Appearance — functional kit mirroring his team, emphasising unity and shared danger.
  • Personality — competent and composed while navigating the complexities of command.
  • Job/role — trusted Expo who led the unit in Lana's absence.
  • Verdict — challenges limited or negative ethnic stereotypes: a character from a diverse background shown in a professional, respected leadership role — part of the show's move away from tokenistic representation.

Danny

Both
  • Appearance — standard police attire, high-visibility vest and utility belt: readiness and duty.
  • Personality — loyal, reliable, steadier and more secure than in series 1; engaged to be married.
  • Job/role — police driver and assistant to the explosives team: the steadfast partner.
  • Verdict — conforms to traditional male traits of strength, reliability and loyalty — yet his supportive role under a female leader quietly challenges the expectation that men lead and women assist.

DS Helen Morgan

Challenges
  • Appearance — professional yet understated clothing; she blends into the investigative environment rather than being styled for the male gaze.
  • Personality — analytical, dedicated, professional and determined.
  • Job/role — detective playing a significant role in the bombing investigation.
  • Verdict — challenges stereotypes as part of the growing representation of competent, resilient women in law enforcement — defined by her work, not her relationship with Thom.

Commander John Francis

Conforms
  • Appearance — suit, tie and badge/lanyard: seniority, formality and distance from the front line.
  • Personality — controlled, decisive, strategic; clipped received-pronunciation delivery signalling rank and class.
  • Job/role — the bureaucratic figurehead overseeing operations from above.
  • Verdict — conforms to conventional portrayals of male leadership in law-enforcement hierarchies: control, decisiveness and authority — the establishment figure Lana's instinct-driven heroism rubs against.

05

Media Language & Key Scenes

The episode constructs a version of reality — realistic in its procedures, exaggerated in its drama. Use VATLs (Visual, Audio, Technical, Language codes) and specific evidence.

Version of reality

Feels real: bomb-disposal procedures, technical language (IED, disrupter, pressure plate), protective gear, radio chatter and call signs, team communication, everyday urban locations (power station, car park) — plus ambient sounds of cars, objects and wind (verisimilitude).

Constructed / exaggerated: events happen back-to-back, constant high-stakes drama, multiple attacks in one day, coincidences (characters personally involved), one person — Lana — seems to solve everything alone, and the bomb defused with one second left: a classic thriller trope.

Top-band sentence: "The extract does not present reality exactly as it occurs, but a selective and intensified version that feels authentic through technical detail and performance while heightening drama to engage the audience."

Night shoots, smoke and debris — gritty realism meets constructed spectacle

Camerawork & editing

  • Close-ups on Lana's face show tension and emotion.
  • Quick cuts during defusal scenes increase suspense.
  • Handheld camera creates panic and urgency.
  • Establishing shots (police HQ, abandoned car park) set the typical crime drama scene.
  • Low-key lighting creates shadows, danger and tension.
  • Tracking shots reveal debris and hiding places — the camera moves behind pillars suggesting hidden threats.

Dialogue & voice

  • Technical terminology creates factual authenticity.
  • Urgent commands ("Take cover!", "Don't move!") mirror real emergency procedure.
  • Overlapping speech and interruptions mimic real emergency communication.
  • Commander Francis' clipped received pronunciation vs Lana's emotionally charged London accent — hierarchy signalled through class and tone.
  • Radio call signs and formal speech codes reflect the procedural tone.

Sort it: Diegetic or Non-diegetic sound?

Diegetic = sound that exists inside the story world. Non-diegetic = added for the audience only.

The ticking of the bomb
Suspenseful music building during a defusal scene
Radio chatter and call signs between officers
Doors slamming; screaming and panic in the street
A low, ominous drone that swells as Lana approaches the device
Lana's dialogue as she takes control of the scene

06

Audience & Theories

Who watches Trigger Point, why, and how do different viewers respond differently? Two theories are essential here: Uses & Gratifications (Blumler & Katz) and Reception Theory (Stuart Hall — MUST KNOW).

Targeting vs Positioning

Targeting: producers use VATLs to attract a preferred audience — e.g. trailers promote Vicky McClure to target her fans (and Line of Duty viewers), and use crime genre conventions to target genre fans.

Positioning: producers use VATLs to make the audience think or feel a certain way — e.g. tense cross-cutting and timers position us to feel how intense a situation is.

Target audience: mainstream adults — plus fans of high-production drama, fans of Vicky McClure and fans of crime drama.

What shapes a response? (GRACCESS)

  • Gender
  • Religion
  • Age — older viewers may find content uncomfortable; younger may be desensitised
  • Cultural experience
  • Cultural competence
  • Ethnicity — beliefs and upbringing
  • Sexuality
  • Situated culture — where and who you watch with

Uses & Gratifications — Blumler & Katz ("Easy as PIES")

Audiences are active — they choose media to satisfy needs. Match each Trigger Point example to its gratification.

1. "A detective may enjoy seeing situations and pressures like their own job on screen."

2. "Trigger Point could show someone what day-to-day life in a bomb squad is like."

3. "The exciting explosions and suspense offer escape from everyday life."

4. "Viewers chat about the cliffhanger with friends the next day — or second-screen while watching."

P.I.E.S — Personal identity · Information · Entertainment · Social relationships

Stuart Hall — Reception Theory

Producers encode texts with values and messages; audiences decode them — but not always as intended. Three readings:

  • Preferred/Dominant — the reading producers hope for: Lana is a heroic, highly skilled bomb disposal expert.
  • Negotiated — the audience accepts the preferred reading but modifies it: Lana is brave and competent, but the series exaggerates or sensationalises terrorism.
  • Oppositional — the audience rejects the preferred reading: the portrayal of security forces as purely heroic is one-sided, fear-mongering, or reinforces negative stereotypes.
ACTIVE — question, interpret, create meaning
PASSIVE — accept messages, easily influenced
Encoded: Lana as hero. But how will different audiences decode her?

⚡ Quick Check — Which reading is it?

1. "A 30-year-old action thriller fan admires Lana's bravery, enjoys the fast-paced explosions, and feels the show represents modern threats realistically."

2. "A viewer rejects the show entirely, seeing the heroic portrayal of security forces as one-sided propaganda that reinforces stereotypes."

3. "A younger viewer enjoys the drama and the characters but feels some parts are too intense and that terrorism is being sensationalised."

4. In reception theory, who ENCODES the text with values and messages?

07

Industry & Context

Scheduling, regulation, funding, marketing, production and distribution — how the industry side of ITV shapes what Trigger Point is and how it reaches us.

📅 Scheduling — why 9pm on a Sunday?

  • Watershed — after 9pm TV can show stronger violence and serious themes suited to older teens and adults.
  • Zoning — the same genre at set times/days: big dramas go late Sunday evening, when audiences relax before the working week and expect high-quality drama.
  • Fragmented audiences — viewers are spread across channels and streamers, so a prime slot pulls a mass audience together at once.
  • Devices — viewers watch live or catch up later on smart TVs, phones and tablets via ITVX.
  • The point of scheduling: to build and keep an audience.

⚖️ Regulation & Funding

  • Ofcom regulates UK TV (and radio, on-demand, telecoms). It acts once at least one complaint is made, and is funded by industry fees plus government grant-in-aid.
  • ITV is a commercial broadcaster — funded by advertising, not a licence fee. Commercial pressure drives audience-friendly content: familiar genres, recognisable actors, cliffhangers.
  • The BBC, by contrast, is funded by the licence fee (£180 per household with a TV).
  • ITV is also a PSB (public service broadcaster) with obligations: regional news, original UK drama, British culture, accessibility (subtitles, audio description), and peak-time content that informs, educates and entertains. Commissioning Trigger Point ticks the "original UK drama" and "British culture" boxes.

📣 Marketing the bomb squad

Traditional advertising: Radio Times & Guardian covers — "Back with a bang!"
A real-time dynamic countdown projected onto London's County Hall — mirroring the show's bomb-squad tension
Star power: writer-producer Jed Mercurio (Line of Duty) is a selling point in himself

How the trailer attracts the audience: explosions, sirens and fast-paced action for instant excitement · tense bomb scenes and time pressure · Vicky McClure to pull in returning fans and Line of Duty viewers · hints of personal trauma for emotional depth · "Who's behind it?" mystery hooks · glimpses of returning characters · high-quality visuals and intense music signalling strong production values.

Also: ITV & cast social media, interactive content and influencer engagement — plus a royal set visit ("the Queen" going behind the scenes) generating free press coverage.

🎬 Production processes

  • How: real London locations → realism; planned action scenes → tension not chaos; serial episodes → weekly cliffhangers; high budget per episode → cinematic look.
  • Who: believable actors; directors whose camera style creates suspense; writers setting a serious tone; police/bomb advisors for accuracy.
  • Tools: CGI explosions (safe but realistic); handheld cameras (panic, urgency); sound design — beeping, breathing (tension); HD filming (gritty realism).
Older crime dramas (The Sweeney)Modern crime dramas (Trigger Point)
Studio filmingReal locations
Simple actionCinematic action
Less realismDetailed procedures
Stand-alone episodesOngoing storylines

🌍 Distribution

  • Distributed internationally by All3Media — sold across six continents.
  • 🇬🇧 ITV1 + ITVX (on-demand, binge-watching, any device) · 🇺🇸 Peacock · 🇨🇦 CBC Gem · 🇦🇺 Stan · 🇳🇿 TVNZ · plus BritBox, CANAL+, HBO Latin America and more.
  • Also available on DVD, and the Chris Roe soundtrack was released by Silva Screen Records.

🕰 Context — how we watch has changed

In the 70s–90s: a handful of channels, the whole family around one set, watch it live or miss it. Now: fragmented audiences, solo viewing on any device, catch-up and bingeing, second-screening on social media. Traditional broadcasters like ITV must evolve how they produce, distribute and market — which is exactly why ITVX, prestige drama and multi-platform marketing campaigns exist. The show also reflects modern social contexts: expectations of gender equality in dangerous jobs (Lana) and ethnic diversity in professional, respected roles.

Exam-Style Practice

The questions we've worked on in class. Try each one from the sentence starters first, then reveal the model to compare.

Q1 · Settings — "How far are the settings typical of a crime drama? Refer to Trigger Point." [10]

Starters: The settings in Trigger Point are typical of a crime drama because… / One way the setting fits the genre is… / However, some parts are not typical because…

The establishing shot of police HQ is typical of the crime drama genre because it presents law enforcement as organised but under constant pressure. The scene shows officers in a secure, open-plan room urgently discussing bomb threats and planning their response. This is typical of crime dramas as police HQs often act as the control centre where serious crimes are analysed, decisions are made quickly, and tension is created through fast-paced dialogue and a sense of ongoing danger.

Q2 · Characters — "How far are the characters in the extract typical of the genre? Explore two characters." [12]

Success criteria: 4–6 pieces of specific evidence · argue typical / not typical / a mix · use media language (representation, stereotypes, camera shots…).

One character in the extract is the protagonist Lana. She is typical of the crime/thriller genre because she is calm under pressure and experienced in dangerous situations. In the extract, she deals with the bomb threat seriously and disregards her own safety to try to stop the second bomb, which is common in this genre. Her role as a bomb disposal officer shows the bravery and responsibility often seen in crime and thriller characters — but also that maverick streak where the hero will ignore orders to do what they feel is right.

Q3 · Version of reality — "How does this extract represent a version of reality? Explore specific aspects of media language." [12]

Top band = show awareness that representations are constructed versions of reality (not just "realistic/unrealistic").

The extract presents a realistic version of reality through its setting: an urban street sealed off with police tape, emergency vehicles, and a bomb disposal unit on site. This mirrors a real-life bomb scare, helping the audience believe in the world of the show while creating tension.

Characters reinforce realism through Lana's professional behaviour — technical language, calm instructions, careful analysis of the device.

However, some moments are exaggerated for drama: the bomb is defused with one second left, a classic thriller trope. In reality teams would evacuate and use remote methods — but producers include it to increase suspense and keep the audience emotionally invested, even if it stretches believability.

Q4 · Contexts — "Explain how media contexts influence crime dramas. Refer to Trigger Point." [10]

Starters: The show reflects modern expectations of gender equality in dangerous jobs, shown when… / Audiences expect to watch on catch-up and devices, so the series is shown on… / The drama reflects social expectations of diversity because…

Gender equality context → Lana as female bomb-disposal lead, calm and authoritative. Digital/technology context → ITVX, catch-up, bingeing, any device. Diversity context → characters from diverse backgrounds in professional, respected roles. Contemporary London context → real locations, modern policing methods, national security fears. Cultural context of high production values → prestige drama competing with streamers.
